payload.question: Is it safe to charge an e-bike battery indoors overnight?

payload.text: Reading the question… the everyday worry about charging an e-bike battery indoors overnight.
Decomposing along five branches: fire-risk data, battery chemistry, charging practice, regulation, insurance.
Fire-risk data anchors the case: London Fire Brigade attended an e-bike or e-scooter battery fire roughly every two days in 2023/24.
Battery chemistry matters too: thermal runaway cannot be put out by normal means, and the vented vapour cloud ignites in seconds.
Flagging the headline safety claim ('a certified pack is safe to charge indoors') for adversarial review — fire-service guidance suggests it may not generalise to overnight, unattended charging.
Adding the certification picture as its own claim: most fires trace to damaged, aftermarket or mismatched chargers and packs, not certified originals.
Insurance branch depends on the indoor-charging claim: exclusion and voided-claim figures inherit its risk.
The scare-story branch ('explodes spontaneously even when not charging') looks weakly sourced and off-topic for a charging question — advocates may struggle.
Claim graph ready: 9 claims, 5 branches, ~18 agents, est £0.90.

claims.text: UK e-bike and e-scooter battery fires rose sharply: London Fire Brigade attended one roughly every two days in 2023/24.
Charging a certified (UL/EN 50604) e-bike battery indoors is safe.
Most e-bike battery fires involve damaged, aftermarket or mismatched chargers and packs, not certified originals.
Once a lithium battery enters thermal runaway it cannot be extinguished by normal domestic means, and the vented vapour cloud can ignite in seconds.
UK regulation lags the risk: there is no mandatory third-party certification for e-bike conversion kits at the point of sale.
Charging in hallways or exits puts the fire between you and the only escape route — the main factor in fatal e-bike fires.
Insurers increasingly exclude or void claims where an uncertified e-bike battery was charged indoors.
E-bike batteries explode spontaneously even when they are not charging.
The safe-practice consensus: charge while awake and present, use the original charger, keep the battery away from exits, and stop at any sign of damage or heat.

payload.text: # Research Verdict — charging an e-bike battery indoors overnight
**Question:** is it safe to charge an e-bike battery indoors overnight?
## The short answer

With the original, certified kit, **yes — with conditions**: certified packs with a working BMS have very low failure rates [3]. But **never overnight or unattended, and never in an escape route**: most fatal fires started while a battery was charging at night [8]. 'Safe indoors' depends on how — and when — you charge.

The risk is real and rising: London Fire Brigade attended an e-bike or e-scooter battery fire roughly every two days in 2023/24 [1]. And regulation lags: there is no mandatory third-party certification for conversion kits at the point of sale [6], so the pack on your landing may never have been independently tested.
## What the fire data shows

Most fires trace to damaged, aftermarket or mismatched chargers and packs, not certified originals [2]; once thermal runaway starts, no domestic means will stop it, and the vented vapour cloud ignites in seconds [4][5]. Location is what kills: charging in a hallway or exit puts the fire between you and the only way out [2]. Where and when you charge is what flips the risk past the headline statistics [8].
## Adjudication
A human juror ruled for the fire-service never-overnight guidance [8] over the blanket certification case [3]; that claim is stamped **human-adjudicated** and its dependents were re-checked.
## Cover and practice implications

Under the adjudicated narrowing [8], the certified-kit case stands for attended, awake-and-present charging [3]; insurers increasingly exclude or void claims where an uncertified pack was charged indoors, so the paperwork follows the practice — and the viral 'explodes spontaneously at rest' line does **not** hold [7]; the consensus is charge awake and present, original charger, away from exits, and stop at any sign of damage or heat [7].
